text: It was upon the seventh night of my vigil that the candle first began to weep. I had set it—oh, with what trembling care!—upon the mantel of black walnut, and watched its flame stand straight and indifferent as a sentinel. Yet now the tallow ran downward in slow and viscid threads, and these threads, I swear it before whatever pitiless God permits such things, were not white but a deep and arterial crimson. Was it madness? You will say it was madness. But tell me—you who have never sat alone with the dead hours pressing upon your skull like wet linen—tell me, then, why the wax should pool upon the floor in the very shape of a hand? A small hand. A child's hand. I pressed my own palm against it and felt, beneath the cooling stuff, a faint and dreadful warmth, a pulse, a quickening, as of something striving upward through the boards to clasp me. I did not scream. I am almost certain I did not scream. I only sat, and watched, and listened to the house settle its old bones about me—and waited for the candle to burn down to the wick, and for the hand to be finished, and for the fingers, at last, to close.

My brother's portrait hung in the eastern gallery, and it was my custom, in those declining autumn afternoons, to stand before it until the light failed. He had been dead these eleven months. The painter—a sallow, secretive man whom I have since been unable to trace—had rendered the likeness with such fidelity that I half expected the painted lips to part and reproach me. And reproach me, in time, they did. For I observed—first with curiosity, then with a creeping and intolerable horror—that the portrait was changing. Not the face! The face remained serene, beatific, abominably calm. It was the eyes. Each evening they had inclined some infinitesimal degree further toward the left—toward the curtained alcove wherein, you understand, no living soul had cause to look. What did he see there? What did he wish me to see? I resisted for a fortnight. Then, upon a moonless night, I took up the lamp and drew the curtain aside. Reader, I will not tell you what crouched within that alcove. I will say only that it wore my brother's coat, and that it had been waiting—patiently, oh so patiently—for me to obey at last the silent summons of those painted, pitiless, ever-watching eyes.

The fever took me in the marshes, and with the fever came the sound. A low respiration—a vast and labouring breath—that rose, as it seemed, from beneath the very fenland, from some leviathan slumbering in the black ooze below the reeds. I told myself it was the wind. There was no wind. I told myself it was my own blood drumming in the chambers of my ears. But blood does not pause, does it? Blood does not hold its breath and listen, as this thing held its breath and listened whenever I dared to move. I lay in the abandoned cottage and counted the inhalations—one, and then another, slower—and I understood, with a clarity that scalded me, that the breathing was matching itself to my own. When I gasped, it gasped. When I stilled myself in terror, it too grew still. And in that silence, more frightful than any sound, I felt the floor beneath my pallet rise—gently, tenderly, as a sleeper's chest will rise—and I knew that I had not taken shelter in a house at all, but had crept, fevered and unknowing, into the open and waiting jaws of the marsh itself, which now drew breath to swallow me down.

I had thought the cellar empty when I sealed it. You will mark that word—thought—for it is the hinge upon which my whole damnation turns. Three courses of brick I laid with my own hands, mortaring each with a care I had never given to any honest labour, and as I worked I hummed, I confess, a foolish little air to drown the silence. But silence, I have learned, cannot be drowned; it can only be deferred. The wall was scarcely dry when the tapping began. A delicate sound—the merest articulation of knuckle upon stone—patient, rhythmic, unmistakably a summons. Three taps. A pause. Three taps. Had I not myself ensured that nothing breathing remained behind that masonry? Yet who, then, knocked? On the second night the tapping acquired a voice—not words, but a sighing, a soft insinuating murmur that pronounced, I grew certain, my own Christian name. By the third I had pressed my ear flat against the cold brick, weeping, pleading for it to cease—and it was then, with my cheek upon the wall, that I felt the answering pressure of a cheek upon the other side, warm through the stone, and heard the murmur say, so very gently: Let me out. Let me out. You know me. Let me out.

The clock in my grandfather's study possessed thirteen hours. I had passed beneath its gilded face a thousand times in childhood and never marked the aberration; but grief sharpens the eye to monstrous particulars, and on the night of the interment I saw it plainly—a thirteenth numeral, struck in tarnished silver where no numeral has any right to dwell. From that hour I could not look away. All through the long watches I sat before it, and the pendulum swung its slow and sickening arc, and I waited—dear Heaven, how I waited!—for the hand to climb past twelve and enter that forbidden region of the dial. Would the world end? Would the dead rise? Would I? When at length it came, there was no chime. There was instead a stillness so absolute that I heard the dust descending through the air. And in that thirteenth hour the room was not the room. The walls had receded into a grey infinitude, and my grandfather stood at the far reach of it, beckoning, his lips moving upon some syllable I could not hear—until the pendulum resumed, and twelve became one, and I found myself screaming at an ordinary clock in an ordinary room, with the ordinary, intolerable knowledge that tomorrow night it would strike thirteen again.
